(Photo source: Ruletkka|Dreamstime.com)

World.title: No agreement over new Wage Law for budgetary sector in Romania
World.content:
The Romanian centrist parties summoned by president Nicusor Dan on August 20 to discuss the new Wage Law for the budgetary sector, a milestone under the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR), failed to reach an agreement. However, the parties will analyse the latest version of the project, presidential adviser Radu Burnete announced after the meeting, as cited by Hotnews.ro.

Acting minister of European projects and investments, who also serves as interim labour minister, Dragos Pislaru, confirmed that the European Commission insisted on an increase of no more than RON 8 billion for the total public payroll in 2027, compared to RON 166 billion in 2026. An increase of RON 12 billion, as envisaged by the latest version of the law, would be acceptable only if budgetary measures are found to compensate for the difference, he explained.

In essence, the Wage Law aims at setting a new set of coefficients for individual wages in the budgetary sector, and a transparent system of bonuses. But as cutting the incomes of specific categories that earn more than they should (a very politically sensitive topic never touched), the wages that are currently lower than they should (under the new, fair coefficients), must be increased significantly.

Separately, the budgetary constraints, particularly relevant in the context of the public debt exceeding the 60% of GDP threshold, prohibit an excessive rise of the overall payroll, thus preventing the convergence towards the desired system of wages in the budgetary sector.

The ongoing negotiations are complicated by the political parties' avoidance of delicate topics and by the Social Democrats’ rhetoric against acting prime minister Ilie Bolojan.

iulian@romania-insider.com

(Photo source: Presidency.ro)

World.title: Romania’s Electrica gets shareholders’ greenlight for EUR 235 mln new power plants
World.content:
The shareholders of the utilities company Electrica (BVB: EL) approved the investment project in Craiova, which provides for the construction of electricity and thermal energy production capacities for the city's centralized heating system and for the industrial consumer Ford Otosan Romania, according to a company’s note to investors.

The total investment value is up to EUR 235 million, plus VAT, for both objectives, according to a report by Electrica submitted to the Bucharest Stock Exchange.

The first objective, with an estimated value of EUR 157.5 million, aims to build a cogeneration plant intended to supply the Centralized Thermal Energy Supply System in Craiova. The second objective, valued at EUR 65.5 million, involves the construction of a plant dedicated to providing thermal energy for technological processes and heating the Ford Otosan Romania industrial platform.

The total value of the project also includes a reserve of approximately 5%, intended to cover possible cost increases during the implementation stage and developments in the energy equipment market, which raises the investment ceiling to EUR 235 million, excluding VAT.

Electrica would finance the investment from secured or unsecured loans and/or from bond issues previously approved by shareholders, within the limit of the EUR 1 billion ceiling approved by the EGMS Decision of April 29, 2026. The company specified that bridge financing can be used until the bonds are issued or loans dedicated to the project, if these will have more advantageous financial conditions, without increasing the total financing ceiling already approved.

iulian@romania-insider.com

World.title: Romania’s Hidroelectrica testing 200 MW hydropower plants on Olt River under pumped regime
World.content:
Romanian hydropower group Hidroelectrica announced it has begun testing the pumped regime of its hydropower plants on Olt River, which have a total capacity of 200 MW. Using the hydropower plants under reversible regime was tested twelve years ago, when the company’s management concluded insufficient economic benefits.

The first of the five such units has been tested under the reversed regime on August 20, as the storage capacity becomes increasingly important as more intermittent renewable generation is added.

Hidroelectrica has in its portfolio, on the Olt, five hydropower plants that can operate in a reversible, pump-turbine system, with a total capacity of 200 MW.

Following the technological tests conducted on August 20, it was concluded that the operation of the hydropower units in pump mode can be achieved under normal operating conditions. The result represents an important element for the further evaluation of the potential of this solution and how it can be integrated into the operation of the existing hydropower infrastructure, the company concluded.

iulian@romania-insider.com

(Photo source: Inquam Photos/Octav Ganea)

World.title: Thaci Expects Acquittal as Hague Court’s War Crimes Verdict Nears
World.content:
Hashim Thaci with co-defendant Rexhep Selimi (R) in court in The Hague, April 2023. Photo: EPA/Koen van Weel/Pool.

Former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci said in an interview broadcast on Thursday evening that he anticipated being acquitted of all charges in the war crimes and crimes against humanity case against him and three other former Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA leaders at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague.

The verdict in the case against Thaci, Kadri Veseli, Rexhep Selimi and Jakup Krasniqi is expected on September 16.

“I expect to be acquitted of every charge. I have nothing to add to the arguments of the defence team or to my final statement in the courtroom,” Thaci said in the written interview with the Pristina-based broadcaster RTV Dukagjini.

The four men are accused of individual and command responsibility for crimes committed against prisoners held at KLA detention facilities in Kosovo and in neighbouring Albania, including 102 murders. The crimes were allegedly committed during and just after the Kosovo War in 1998 and 1999.

All four defendants have pleaded not guilty.

Thaci said he did not regret supporting the creation of the Kosovo Specialist Chambers when he was in office, but said he had not expected the decision by Kosovo’s elected representatives to be “misused so brutally”.

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was created specifically to try former members of the KLA. It is located in The Hague and staffed by international judges and prosecutors due to doubts about the Kosovo justice system’s ability to try former KLA fighters, many of whom are considered heroes in Kosovo.

In the interview, Thaci spoke about a 2010 report by former Swiss Council of Europe rapporteur Dick Marty, which alleged serious crimes including organ-trafficking by KLA-linked figures. The report ultimately led to the establishment of the Kosovo Specialist Chambers. Thaci claimed that its allegations were developed with the involvement of officials at the Council of Europe from Serbia and Russia – both of which oppose Kosovo’s independence.

“The freedom and the construction of Kosovo’s independence were unswallowable for Serbia and Russia. After failing to delegitimise it at the International Court of Justice [which ruled that Kosovo’s independence declaration did not violate international law], they turned to the Council of Europe. The aim was clear: to discredit the state of Kosovo,” he said.

Thaci also criticised the prosecution’s treatment of defence witnesses and evidence in his trial.

He accused prosecutors of giving greater weight to what he described as “fabricated testimony” originating from the time when Slobodan Milosevic was in power in Belgrade, and dismissing testimony from senior Western and international officials who were “the eyes and ears” in Kosovo.

“The prosecution is elevating evidence fabricated during the era of the Milosevic regime, and ignoring the testimony of senior officials from the US, NATO, Britain, the UN, the OSCE and other international institutions,” he said.

Thaci noted that the appearance of such international figures as defence witnesses demonstrated their concern about the proceedings.

“It is not easy for these personalities to sit in such a courtroom. I understood that they were seeing that something wrong was happening in this process. They felt a moral obligation to tell the truth,” he said.

Thaci declined to comment on the current Kosovo government’s approach to the Specialist Chambers.

Asked whether his rights had been violated during the proceedings, he replied that he considered the “process as a whole” to have involved violations.

He also criticised the decision not to release him on bail, saying that the arguments used against his release were based on “prejudices and hypotheses”. Thaci said several NATO member states had offered guarantees on his behalf and that he remained grateful to them.

During the trial, the prosecution attempted to prove that, as members of the KLA General Staff, they were responsible for lower-ranking fighters who committed crimes. The defence argued that the KLA did not have a proper army command structure, so the defendants did not have real authority over lower-ranking KLA fighters.

Thaci resigned as Kosovo’s president in November 2020 to face the charges and together with the other three men was sent to detention in The Hague, where they have been ever since. The trial started in April 2023.

During the trial, KLA veterans and their supporters have staged protests in Pristina, Tirana, Skopje, Strasbourg and The Hague, accusing the Specialist Chambers of bias.

In 2024, Thaci was also charged with obstruction of justice, alongside four others, including former Kosovo Justice Minister Hajredin Kuci. The trial for this case started in February, days after proceedings in the war crimes and crimes against humanity trial ended. Thaci and the four others accused of obstruction of justice – Kuci, Isni Kilaj, Bashkim Smakaj and Fadil Fazliu – have denied wrongdoing.

World.title: Democracy Digest: Hungary’s Public Media News Back on Air as Magyar Marks 100 days
World.content:
Budget talks underway; location of Prague’s ‘mega-hospital’ confirmed; norovirus outbreak suspected at Czech spa

The Czech government held its first post-summer recess cabinet meeting on Monday, with the 2027 budget top of the agenda. Throughout the week, ministers have been holding one-on-one talks with Finance Minister Alena Schillerova, with many of them emerging from the closed talks with promises of budget increases for their individual portfolios. Talks are still in the preliminary stages, and the draft budget should be submitted by the government by the end of September, with the ruling ANO party flagging healthcare and transport infrastructure as its two top priorities. Looking at some of the key announcements, Defence Minister Jaromir Zuna of the far-right SPD party said he expects defence spending to increase to 191 billion Czech crowns (about 7.9 billion euros) next year, thus reaching 2 per cent of GDP in contrast to this and the previous year. On the culture front, Minister Oto Klempir said he was striving to increase his department’s budget to 20 billion crowns (around 825 million euros) in 2027. And while the Culture Ministry has long been expected to start funding directly Czech public media from January next year as the government prepares to scrap licence fees, recent statements from officials close to finance chief Schillerova suggest a new model might be chosen: specifically, that the cancellation of licence fees might first be postponed, and that the nearly 8 billion crowns intended for Czech TV and Czech Radio would come not from the Culture Ministry, but from the General Treasury Administration – a separate chapter for public expenses that are not assigned to specific ministries in advance that includes, for instance, emergency funding to deal with natural disasters.

A key campaign promise of the current government, the Czech capital’s future “mega-hospital” will be built on the grounds of the current Kralovske Vinohrady University Hospital (FNKV) in Prague, the government announced this week. “It’s not like the entire campus will be demolished, we will only use part of the campus where there’s currently unused land,” vowed Health Minister Adam Vojtech as he unveiled the wide-ranging plans for the new hospital, where some of the current FNKV departments along with those of other Prague hospitals are set to be relocated. Just weeks ago, the government commissioned the ministries of health and defence to transfer the land to the Defence Ministry by the end of August. Plans to designate the new facility as a military hospital to include the costs in reported defence expenditures – and meet NATO requirements – have been met with scepticism by some who point out that mostly civilians will be treated there, and that Prague already has the Central Military Hospital (UVN).

The Regional Hygiene Station of the Olomouc region, in eastern Czechia, confirmed four new cases of people falling ill with what initial findings suggest could be noroviruses, bringing the total number of cases to 115 patients since the start of the outbreak at the Priessnitz spa in Jesenik earlier this month. “The regional hygiene station is recording a decrease in the number of newly reported cases,” a spokeswoman said, pointing to the effectiveness of the anti-epidemic measures taken by regional authorities and the spa’s management since the first cases began emerging, and highlighting that the risk of transmission to the wider population remained low. “Within a few days we managed to prevent the spread of the infection”, meanwhile assured the spa’s director Roman Provaznik, who also criticised the spread of fake news and alarmist statements on social media about the situation at his establishment. The cause of the outbreak remains unclear to date, however, and lab examinations are still ongoing to determine how more than 100 people fell ill with intestinal flu-like symptoms.

World.title: Could Trump’s Administration Force a Deal on Bosnia’s State Property?
World.content:
As the issue of the ownership of state and defence property goes to the very core of sovereignty in Bosnia and Herzegovina, it has evaded a neat and lasting solution. For years, international interest has wavered, leaving the question to be answered at a later and hopefully more favourable date.

Today, however, with Washington increasingly driven by business motives in energy, mining and other critical infrastructure, there is mounting concern that the US could seek to drive through a settlement that is ultimately detrimental to the country’s fundamental interests.

World.title: Waste Money Wasted: The Millions of Euros Behind Albania’s Ghost Incinerators
World.content:
Garbage trucks pull up every day at the landfill that serves the Albanian capital, next to Sharra cemetery in the Erzen Valley. The pile of waste grows ever higher, sometimes catching fire and emitting clouds of pungent smoke.

It wasn’t supposed to be like this.

The promotional videos depicted a futuristic complex of two glass pyramids supported by a metal structure, where the waste would be incinerated.

Instead, nine years after the contract for the incinerator was signed, the people who said they’d build it went on trial in mid-July, accused of pocketing tens of millions of euros in public funds that should have been spent on finally solving the problem of Tirana’s waste.

Of the 12 accused, alleged masterminds Mirel Mertiri and Klodian Zoto are on the run.

World.title: ‘Return Hubs’ for Migrants Anticipated in Balkans for ‘Era of Deportations’
World.content:
The infrastructure is already there. With generous help from the EU, Balkan countries have built a network of detention and reception centres to hold migrants over the last decade. Some, including Bosnia and Serbia, already have agreements with EU members to accommodate their migrants.

“There are quite a lot of camps that are fully equipped with beds and everything needed. So, they [the currently inactive detention centres] can very easily be put in use again within 24 or 48 hours, very quickly,” said Milica Svabic, a lawyer at the Belgrade-based KlikAktiv, an NGO providing legal support to migrants and asylum seekers.

The new EU return regulations are yet to come into force. After European Council and European Parliament negotiators reached a deal on the regulations on June 1, MEPs officially adopted them on June 16. But the new rules still must be signed off by the Council of the European Union before they come into force.

The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights and a number of human rights organisations have strongly condemned the regulations, warning that outsourcing detention to ‘third countries’ outside the European bloc bypasses fundamental human rights protections.

However, some EU member states, such as the Netherlands, Greece, Austria, Germany and Denmark, have already started exploring arrangements with third countries. As yet, there is no official confirmation on which countries these may be.

Western European governments are under domestic political pressure, exacerbated by the surge in popularity of far-right parties, to exert much stronger control over migration and deport migrants if they have no legal basis to remain.

The European Commission told BIRN that “a few member states launched an initiative looking into return hubs earlier this year”.

“The Commission has been invited as an observer, and we are following discussions closely … The Commission is not negotiating any such agreement or arrangement,” it said in a written response.

Nicholas Ioannides, deputy minister for migration in Cyprus, which currently holds the presidency of the Council of the European Union, said in June that the plan is to set up these hubs “maybe in Africa or Asia”, but “not close to European borders”.

Some Western Balkan leaders have previously rejected the idea of hosting return hubs, most notably when Britain explored the same option with unnamed countries in the region, as the BBC reported last year.

While Kosovo’s Prime Minister Albin Kurti expressed openness towards the idea, Albania has heavily criticised the concept of return hubs, even though it has set up migrant holding camps for use by Italy. Montenegro’s Prime Minister Milojko Spajic said in October 2025 that his country will not be hosting rejected asylum seekers from Britain.

Nikola Kovacevic, a Serbian lawyer who has represented refugees for more than a decade, told BIRN that if return hubs are located in the Western Balkans, the EU will “send people who have a terrible situation, but don’t meet requirements for asylum”, while “simultaneously testing” whether the state to which they are to be returned is a safe enough.

Kovacevic argued, however, that “Serbia, as a country which cannot effectively protect the human rights of refugees and asylum seekers, is not a safe third country”.

World.title: Remains of 23 Wartime Victims Unearthed from Mass Graves in Kosovo
World.content:
Kosovo Police guards the mass grave location in Kalluder village on July 30, 2026. Photo: BIRN.

As forensic experts near the completion of weekslong excavations at three locations in the villages of Kalluder and Jabuke in northern Kosovo near Zubik Potok, authorities announced on Thursday that they have unearthed remains believed to belong to 23 individuals who have been missing since the 1998-99 war.

The identities of the victims will be determined following forensic examinations.

Acting Interior Minister Xhelal Svecla stated that the “remains of 23 individuals have been found in three mass grave locations”, believed to belong to Kosovo Albanian civilians who were forcibly disappeared during the war.

“Kosovo demands accountability about the masterminds, perpetrators, those who concealed the bodies, and those who hid information about the whereabouts of these bodies,” Svecla said.

“Serbia’s silence is concerning and this silence is open support for planners, organisers and perpetrators,” he added.

The excavations in Zubin Potok began on July 28.

Agron Limani, head of Kosovo’s Government Commission on Missing Persons, said the remains were found at three locations in the villages of Kalluder and Jabuke.

“The remains of 23 people have been found. So far, 20 have been exhumed and the final three are being recovered today. We hope the process will be concluded today,” Limani told BIRN on Thursday.

At the first site in Kalluder, the remains of 13 people were found and then transferred to the Institute of Forensic Medicine. The remains of four people were found at a site in Jabuke, while the remains of six were found at another location in Kalluder.

“The third location, in Kalluder, is around 300-400 metres from the first one. Six bodies have been found, three have been recovered and the remaining three are expected to be recovered today and transferred to Forensics,” Limani noted.

Kosovo’s Special Prosecution Office said on Wednesday that teams from the Institute of Forensic Medicine had identified skeletal remains believed to belong to at least 23 individuals.

“Full identification will be carried out after the completion of forensic examinations and the relevant procedures,” the prosecution said.

On July 29, acting Prime Minister Albin Kurti said that the authorities’ immediate suspicion upon locating the remains was that they could belong to a group of 23 intellectuals who disappeared during the war.

“Our immediate suspicion when we learned that mortal remains had been found was that it was the group of 23 intellectuals in Mitrovica who were kidnapped and forcibly disappeared. We must wait for our institutions to determine exactly what has been found there,” Kurti said.

Three individuals – J.R., M.J. and M.B. – are currently in detention in connection with the case on suspicion of committing war crimes against the civilian population.

A report published on July 29, 2026 by Kosovo’s Institute for Crimes Committed During the War notes that 1,578 people remain missing.

Kosovo authorities and families of missing persons have repeatedly called on Serbia to provide information and open its archives about the locations of burial sites of people forcibly disappeared during the war.

World.title: Montenegro Opposition Leader Claims PM Spajic is Serbian Army Reservist
World.content:
Montenegrin opposition leader Milan Knezevic on Thursday presented documents that he alleged show that Prime Minister Milojko Spajic sought to join Serbia’s military reserve and was subsequently accepted.

Knezevic called for Spajic’s resignation and questioned how a member of the Serbian armed forces could serve as prime minister of a NATO member state, Montenegro.

Knezevic, leader of the Democratic People’s Party, which until recently was part of the ruling parliamentary majority and which has close ties to Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic, displayed three documents at a news conference in Podgorica.

He said the first showed Spajic applied on February 17, 2023 to become a member of the Serbian military reserve, while the other two allegedly confirmed his admission and obliged him to report for duty if required. The documents’ authenticity could not be independently verified.

Knezevic claimed the papers had been provided by “disappointed” members of Spajic’s Europe Now movement.

He accused the prime minister of violating several laws and deceiving the public.

Spajic responded to the allegations by accusing Knezevic of “obediently carrying out the tasks of his (in)formal boss from Belgrade” – a reference to Serbian leader Vucic – in an effort to slow Montenegro’s path towards the European Union.

“It is sad to watch a man who was indisputably rhetorically talented and interesting in the past,” Spajic wrote on X.

The allegations come amid a renewed dispute over Spajic’s ties to Serbia and his citizenship status.

In February 2023, Spajic’s candidacy for Montenegro’s presidential election was rejected by the State Election Commission after information emerged that he held Serbian citizenship and had maintained residence in Serbia.

Spajic said at the time that he had submitted a request to renounce his Serbian citizenship and had deregistered his Serbian residence.

His candidacy was ultimately rejected, and the Europe Now movement replaced him with Jakov Milatovic, who went on to win the presidential election.

Knezevic also alleged that Spajic had received political backing from Serbian President Vucic, before later turning against him.

Knezevic called on President Milatovic and EU ambassador Johan Sattler to address the allegations.

There was no public response from Serbian officials by the time of publication of this article.

World.title: Human Rights Watchdog Urges Italy, Albania to End Offshore Migrant Detention
World.content:
Italian police officers outside a fenced entrance at Gjader port in Albania, deployed as security for the arrival of migrants transferred by sea. Photo: BIRN/Nensi Bogdani.

The human rights organisation Amnesty International on Thursday called on Italy and Albania to end a deal designed to send migrants and asylum seekers to offshore detention in Albania.

In a new research report, Amnesty International said that the 2023 deal between Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama, “is jeopardising people’s safety, liberty and human rights”.

Under the scheme, adult males from countries designated as “safe“ who are intercepted by the Italian coastguard while attempting to cross the Mediterranean would be transferred by ship to detention centres in Albania, which are run under Italian jurisdiction. There, their asylum claims would be fast-tracked and completed within 28 days – far shorter than the months-long process typical in Italy – before likely repatriation.

“Offshore detention is ultimately aimed at deterrence and trying to shift and evade both the responsibilities of responding to people migrating and the obligation to provide asylum to those who need it. Italy’s deal with Albania shows yet again the unavoidable human rights costs of this approach,” said Eve Geddie, director of Amnesty International’s European Institutions Office, said in a press release.

“Just before the deal entered into force, Amnesty International sounded the alarm on the harmful impact it would inevitably have on the rights of people in distress at sea, and of people transferred to Albania. Clearly, these concerns have now materializsed,” Geddie’s statement added.

Italian courts ordered the first three groups that were sent to Albania be returned to Italy, citing an EU Court of Justice (CJEU) ruling from October 4, 2024, that a “safe country” designation must apply to the entire national territory.

In March 2025, Meloni abandoned the original plan pending a resolution of legal challenges. The Italian government then approved legislation instead allowing migrants and refugees issued with deportation orders from Italian authorities to be detained in Gjader, Albania.

The shift means that the Gjader camp has been converted into a repatriation centre for holding those who reached Italy, were rejected for asylum and then issued deportation orders.

According to Amnesty International’s research, 500 men have been “forcibly transferred to the Albanian detention centre in Gjader over the past 15 months.”

The report noted that “between 11 April and 16 May 2025, 42 critical incidents were recorded in the Gjader centre, including at least two attempted hangings, a protest where three people were injured from shattered glass, and various self-harm incidents.

“The Italian government has obstructed independent monitoring of the Agreement’s implementation, including by restricting parliamentary oversight and bypassing ordinary legislative processes. By limiting access and oversight by independent rights observers, what happens in the Albanian detention centres remains largely shrouded in secrecy,” the report said.

“Whilst people detained in Albania fall under Italian jurisdiction, their physical distance from Italy combined with limited access to lawyers, courts and other safeguards, significantly undermines the effectiveness of the right to seek asylum and to access justice,” the report added.

A BIRN investigation found that the cost of constructing the centres in Shengjin and Gjader almost doubled from 39.2 million euros to over 74 million, while the average cost per bed in Albania reached around 72,000 euros. The investigation also found that the entire procedure was conducted through direct negotiation and without competition.

World.title: Croatian Landlords Fight New Rules, Protests Looming?
World.content:
August the 21st, 2026 – Croatian landlords are fighting against the new rules, with potential protests on the horizon. They’ve even reported the new law to the European Commission.

Index reports that the landlords’ association Spasimo male obiteljske iznajmljivače (SMOi – Save Small Family Landlords) has filed an official objection with the European Commission against the proposed new Croatian Hospitality Activity Act through the EU’s TRIS notification system. The association claims that certain provisions of the draft law are not in line with EU law and is asking the European Commission to examine them before the law is adopted by the Croatian Parliament.

They have taken particular issue with the mandatory re-categorisation of accommodation every decade, the new rules for “host” status, and the obligation for landlords in multi-apartment buildings to obtain the consent of two-thirds of the co-owners and every immediate neighbour in order to rent out their property.

“one nuisance neighbour can shut down your business”

According to the aforementioned association, under the proposed law a single immediate neighbour could prevent the continuation of short-term rental activity, even if the majority of co-owners support the landlord. This would also apply to existing landlords who have been operating legally for years. If they fail to obtain the required consents by the end of 2029, they could lose the right to operate.

“We’re not against maintaining proper order in buildings, control, and the protection of residents. However, the state must prove with analyses and data where the problem really exists, how big it is, and why it cannot be solved with milder measures: inspections and supervision based on reports, enforcement of house rules, and sanctions for actual violations,” the association said.

“If there’s noise, disorder, or breach of regulations, then the state must react quickly and strictly and equally toward everyone. However, the decision to revoke the right to work may only be made by the competent public authority, based on facts, and not by a neighbour without any explanation.”

croatian landlords strongly oppose re-categorisation

SMOi also objects to the proposed re-categorisation of accommodation every ten years, regardless of whether the property has been modified in the meantime. They claim the procedure would cover more than 125,000 properties and more than 150,000 categorised accommodation units, with the costs borne by the landlords themselves. The association notes that the new categorisation criteria are still unknown because the Ministry of Tourism and Sport will set them later by ordinance. While they do not dispute the state’s right to control safety and quality, they see no justification for automatically re-checking all landlords.

“host status” faces scrutiny…

The association criticises the provision that would tie “host” status to a person’s residence in the same county as the accommodation. They argue this treats landlords differently depending on where they live and that landlords in multi-apartment buildings are excluded from this status even if they meet other conditions. SMOi says such distinctions are unrelated to the quality of service provided.

portugal and ireland have already scrapped these ideas?

The association cites Portugal and Ireland as examples of countries where contested provisions of regulations were changed during the EU notification procedure. “Croatia should not introduce a stricter model than the one Portugal already abandoned due to inconsistency with the EU acquis. The examples of Portugal and Ireland prove that citizens’ engagement can significantly influence the final version of a law,” said SMOi president Vedran Tomić, calling on Croatian landlords to participate in the TRIS procedure and submit their comments.

are protests coming in the future? potentially…

The association argues that restrictions on tourist rentals should not be applied uniformly across the whole of Croatia, from the most tourist-burdened cities to depopulated and economically weaker areas.

“Let’s not kid ourselves here, the problem of mass tourism doesn’t lie at the hands of family accommodation, nor is the goal of these measures affordable housing,” said association vice-president Hana Matić. “We’d like to call on everyone to stop turning a blind eye to the systematic favouring of institutional investors for whose benefit numerous laws are being changed, including the Hospitality Activity Act, all to the detriment of Croatian citizens and the future of our children. The first step is a comment in the TRIS system, and public protests are becoming increasingly likely,” she concluded.

World.title: Croatian Food Prices Could be Even Higher Next Year
World.content:
August the 21st 2026 – Croatian food prices could end up being even higher next year as extreme weather causes tremendous problems for domestic production.

Adviser to the Minister of Agriculture Tatjana Radić warned that the consequences of this year’s drought on food prices could become strongly visible next year, with a possible price increase of 20 to 30 percent, and according to some estimates even up to 40 percent. Appearing on the main news programme of Croatian Radio Television (HRT), Poslovni reports that Radić spoke about climate change, irrigation, dependence on imports and the proposal of the Croatian Chamber of Agriculture to establish a national fund that would finance the adaptation of agriculture to climate change.

“Additional investments in agriculture and in security are always welcome. The Croatian Chamber of Agriculture already sent letters during the third amendments to the Strategic Plan about the establishment of a joint risk fund, which also led to changes in the plan. Progress can also be made in this area by farmers joining forces, with the state adding an extra 20 percent of funds,” Radić said.

climate change is happening more rapidly than we can keep up with

Radić believes that Croatia is not necessarily lagging behind the rest of Europe when it comes to adapting to climate change because, as she says, the entire continent is facing similar problems.

“I wouldn’t say we’re lagging behind. The whole of Europe is currently in crisis when it comes to climate change. We are all applying different practices and using different interventions to adapt to these changes. However, the speed of these changes is much greater than can currently be kept up with. Some things were expected, and some were unexpected,” she said, before adding that Croatian farmers have been suffering the consequences of drought, hail and other weather disasters for years.

“Croatian farmers have been fighting drought for the seventh year already; they’re fighting hail and various climate disasters that damage their incomes and productivity. The fact is that this is production under the open sky and that farmers need help,” she said.

retailers need to do their bit

Radić believes that, in addition to climate change, Croatian agriculture is also threatened by growing dependence on imports in general. “When it comes to imports, consumers themselves largely decide. The fact is that we have lower purchasing power, but at the same time, when we talk about the price of pork, we can see that the price of a kilogram of meat is almost the same as the price of a coffee in a cafe,” she stated, calling on retail chains to increase the share of domestic products and make it easier for Croatian producers to access the market.

“There are very many Croatian products available. You can see the Proven Quality label, meat from Croatian farms and other labels for our products in retail chains. We’re therefore calling on retail chains to increase their overall share of domestic products and enable Croatian producers greater access to the market. There are also online services and various channels through which our customers can get domestic products,” she said.

issues with the fragmented land are affecting irrigation

One of the biggest problems in adapting to droughts is the weak development of irrigation systems. Radić cites the fragmentation of agricultural land and high technology prices as key obstacles.

“Croatian farms and land are fragmented. We have to be aware of the fact that on one hectare we sometimes have four or five plots. When we talk about an average of ten hectares, or 15 hectares in Europe, here you sometimes find 70 different parcels. In order to consolidate production, you first have to resolve the issue of land and connecting it,” she explained.

She also warned about the problem of rising prices of agricultural equipment when available subsidies increase.“We often talk about giving subsidies to farmers, but they invest that money in new technologies and pay those who sell them. It has often happened that the prices of those technologies increase when it becomes clear how high the level of subsidy is. Too little is said about this, and it should be talked about a lot,” she said.

croatian food prices could increase in 2027

Radić believes that the consequences of the prolonged drought could be felt more strongly next year. “On the one hand we had price dumping at the state level; surpluses were coming to us from various sides and imported goods that were pushing down our prices. Now we can see a trend of slight growth. What we will definitely perhaps feel next year is the consequence of this drought, which has never been at this level. Estimates are very difficult to make, but in our conversations an increase of 20 to 30 percent is mentioned, and it could reach 40 percent,” she said.

Omiš farmers will get subsidies

Radić also commented on farmers whose property was damaged in the major fire in the Omiš area.

“It’s very important that they follow the pages of the Ministry of Agriculture, where all the notices have been published. We also have information that the Ministry of Finance has raised this issue and that help will be provided to the burned areas and our farmers. That is a big thing for them, because we have to protect them,” she said. “What happened could have happened across a much larger area, and then we would really be in big trouble. Even as it is, we are in serious trouble,” she concluded.

World.title: Victoria’s Secret is Officially Coming to Croatia
World.content:
August the 21st, 2026 – Victoria’s Secret, a massive brand loved by women all around the world is set to open its doors in Croatia, more specifically in Zagreb.

Poslovni reports that Alshaya plans to open its first store in Croatia in the fourth quarter of 2026. The opening of the store represents expansion into Central and Eastern Europe, where the Alshaya Group already operates several brands in the Czech Republic, Poland and Romania.

The Alshaya Group, one of the world’s leading operators of brand franchises, today announced its entry into Croatia, which will become the Group’s 21st market, marking another important milestone in Alshaya’s continuous growth. Alshaya plans to open its first store in Croatia in the fourth quarter of 2026, debuting with Victoria’s Secret at Arena Centre (Centar) in Zagreb. The opening builds on the growing eCommerce business that Alshaya already runs for the brand in Croatia. Alshaya first introduced Victoria’s Secret in the MENA region in 2010 and over the past 16 years has expanded its long-standing partnership with the brand to 11 markets.

The opening will bring the Victoria’s Secret in-store experience to customers in Croatia, complementing the brand’s existing online presence in the market and offering customers greater choice and access to the brand.

The Alshaya Group offers an unparalleled selection of more than 50 favourite international brands to customers across the Middle East and North Africa (MENA), Turkey and Europe, with over 3,500 stores, cafés, restaurants and leisure destinations. Today’s announcement marks entry into the fourth market in Central and Eastern Europe (CEE), where it already operates Victoria’s Secret and Bath & Body Works stores in the Czech Republic, Poland and Romania.

John Hadden, CEO of the Alshaya Group, said: “We’re very excited to announce the start of our journey in Croatia and look forward to opening our first store with Victoria’s Secret. We know that customers in Croatia are excited about the brand following the recent launch of our Victoria’s Secret online store, and we hope to bring many more of our brands to the country in the coming years.”

Back in April this year, the Alshaya Group announced that it had taken over the licensed Starbucks business for Greece and Cyprus, becoming the new exclusive owner and operator of the business, and in July the company opened the first Starbucks cafe in Georgia.

Alshaya Group is otherwise a dynamic family-owned company founded in Kuwait back in 1890.

With consistent growth and innovation, the company is one of the world’s leading operators of brand franchises, offering customers an unparalleled selection of more than 50 favourite international brands. The Alshaya Group portfolio spans the Middle East and North Africa (MENA), Turkey and Europe, with over 3,500 stores, cafés, restaurants and leisure destinations, major logistics and food production facilities, as well as more than 125 online and digital businesses, including one of the region’s largest retail loyalty programmes, Aura. Operating across multiple sectors including fashion, food, health and beauty, pharmacy, and hospitality and entertainment, more than 50,000 Alshaya employees are united by a commitment to delivering authentic excellence in customer service and brand experiences.

From leading stores and restaurants in prestigious shopping centres to local cafes, drive-thrus and online sales, Alshaya Group brings customers the experiences they want with the brands they love, in the ways they choose – including Starbucks, American Eagle, Foot Locker, Victoria’s Secret, H&M, Bath & Body Works, Charlotte Tilbury, Raising Cane’s, Shake Shack, Chipotle, Primark and Ulta Beauty.

World.title: Croatia Must Focus on Value for Money & Not Just Visitor Numbers
World.content:
August the 21st, 2026 – Croatia now needs to focus much more on actual value for money and not just counting visitor numbers constantly.

Currently, Croatia’s tourism capacities are well occupied, but the real contest will be in the “value for money” category. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that physically speaking, the country is very close to the limit when it comes to tourist visits, but work needs to be done on quality. That is the message being heard in recent weeks from officials, tourism workers and analysts. As far as the numbers are concerned, those for the first seven months show stability. June under-performed, but May and July were exceptionally good.

According to data from the eVisitor system, which covers tourist traffic realised in commercial and non-commercial facilities as well as nautical charter (eCrew system), Croatia recorded 12.4 million arrivals and 59.1 million overnight stays in the period from January to the end of July. Compared with the same period last year, this represents growth of 1 percent in both arrivals and overnight stays.

different methodologies

Of that total, 56.1 million overnight stays were realised on the Adriatic coast and on the islands, representing growth of 0.5 percent compared with last year, while more than 3 million overnight stays were recorded on the mainland, including the city of Zagreb, which is 1 percent more than last year. Looking at individual markets, during the first seven months the largest number of overnight stays were generated by guests from Germany (10.3 million), Croatia (7.6 million), Slovenia (6.7 million), Austria (4.3 million), Poland (3.9 million), the Czech Republic (3 million), the UK (2.2 million), Hungary (2.1 million) and others.

higher revenue per overnight stay is needed

The focus will increasingly have to shift to the quality of tourism growth: how much revenue is generated per overnight stay and whether guests are satisfied with the value they receive.

eVisitor data also show that in July this year Croatia recorded 4.7 million arrivals and 29.6 million overnight stays, representing growth of 2.5 percent in arrivals and 1 percent in overnight stays compared with July last year. In the seventh month the largest numbers of guests came from Germany, Slovenia, Croatia, Poland, the Czech Republic, Austria, Hungary and others. By counties, Istria, Split-Dalmatia County and Kvarner recorded the most tourists, while the most visited destinations were Rovinj, Vir, Poreč, Medulin and Dubrovnik. Of course, these statistics are not perfectly comparable because different countries use somewhat different methodologies. Nevertheless, they show a broader trend.

Croatia is not competing in some isolated contest and must increasingly compete not only with its coastline and accommodation capacities, but also on price, quality, accessibility and the overall value that tourists believe they receive for their money. Despite the “gloomy mood” that can often be read about in the media or on social networks, Croatian tourism is not collapsing. At the same time, it would be difficult to describe the current season as some kind of extraordinary boom.

“The numbers indicate that the tourism sector is operating at a very high level, but that physical growth has slowed significantly. Arrivals and overnight stays are still growing, but only marginally, while there is high volatility between individual months. The season so far, during the pre-season and the summer season, has been fairly good. The real test remains August and September, which will be strongly influenced by last-minute promotions and bookings. At the moment the industry is progressing steadily and, although the growth rates are not the same as those recorded during the period of rapid expansion before 2020, they are building on a much higher base,” says InterCapital analyst Mihael Antolić.

Improved results in domestic tourism are something to be praised, as is the gradual diversification of foreign source markets. At the same time, the growth in nominal tourism revenues is also encouraging, provided it is not driven almost entirely by higher prices. On the other hand, the shortening of the average stay, the very high seasonality of the sector, the concentration of tourism along the coast and the increasing focus on the price-quality ratio point to problems that will have to be addressed in the coming years.

“In other words, the question for Croatia is probably no longer how to attract as many additional tourists as possible. With more than 59 million overnight stays in just the first seven months, the sector is already operating at a very high level. Instead, the focus will increasingly have to shift to the quality of tourism growth: how much revenue is generated per overnight stay, whether guests are satisfied with the value they receive, whether the season can be extended beyond July and August, and whether more tourist activity can be distributed across the rest of the country,” Antolić is clear.

croatia must actually put value for money in focus

It remains to be seen whether tourism revenues in Croatia can continue to grow in the medium term, especially as other countries across the Mediterranean become more competitive, Antolić adds.

“However, for now the numbers do not actually support either of the two extremes that often appear in headlines. Croatian tourism is neither collapsing nor recording some extraordinary new boom. Instead, it appears to be stabilising at historically high levels, with slower volume growth and stronger value growth becoming the new reality,” Antolić concludes.

World.title: Conference League Play-Offs: Hajduk and Raków Draw 2-2 at Poljud
World.content:
Hajduk took on Raków tonight at Poljud in the first leg of the Conference League play-off round. Gonzalo Garcia’s side are two matches away from securing a spot in the group phase of the European competition, with the return leg set for next Thursday in Częstochowa at 7 pm.

Hajduk’s opponent is anything but easy, and virtually everyone in Split is well aware of that. It has been a staggering 16 years since Hajduk last enjoyed a European autumn campaign, and in that time the club has never been closer to a return to continental football. That is precisely why tonight’s match, for which Poljud saw demand outstrip ticket availability, carried such significance.

Lineups

Hajduk: Silic – Sigur, Maresic, Raci, Hrgovic – Pukstas, Pajaziti – Bamba, Dalisson, Soticek – Sego

Rakow: Trelowski – Tudor, Racovitan, Svarnas – Ameyaw, Kochergin, Repka, Ouma – Diaby-Fadiga, Emreli, Kwiatkowski

Match report

The match kicked off in a fantastic atmosphere at packed Poljud, with Hajduk chasing a place in the Conference League. It got off to a lively start — in the 4th minute, Bamba intercepted a pass from the visitors’ defense and burst into the penalty area, where he was impeded by Svarnas. Referee Očenaš waved play on, though, much to the loud disapproval of the home crowd.

In the 11th minute came the first real moment of danger at the Hajduk end. Ameyaw whipped in a cross, but Emreli caught goalkeeper Toni Silić in the head instead of the ball. The Split shot-stopper needed treatment as a result.

In the 17th minute, Bamba broke away down the left, using his pace to full effect before whipping in a low, first-time cross for Šego, whose effort was blocked, leaving Hajduk with a corner. The hosts worked it quickly from the resulting set piece in the 18th minute, with a well-rehearsed routine picking out Dalisson, though his shot lacked precision.

Hajduk deservedly took the lead in the 21st minute. Bamba delivered a cross for Šego, who timed his run to perfection, arrived unmarked at the far post and calmly nodded home to send Poljud into raptures!

Hajduk continued to press aggressively across every line in the 26th minute, which brought them another corner — again worked towards Dalisson, but once more the Spaniard’s effort lacked.

Raków levelled almost out of nothing in the 27th minute. Otieno powered past everyone down the left, crossed for Emreli, who nodded it home past Silić. It was 1-1.

In the 31st minute, Bamba — putting in an excellent performance, a constant threat and already with an assist to his name — won a yellow card for Otieno, the visitors’ provider for their goal. Two minutes later, Šimun Hrgović also picked up a booking for a foul from behind on the opposite side of the pitch. The impression is that the referee is reaching for early cards in an attempt to keep the players calm and maintain control and authority over the match.

In the 40th minute came a big scramble in front of the Hajduk goal, as Raków showcased their biggest weapon — set pieces. They whipped a delivery into the heart of the penalty area, but the resulting effort was blocked by one of their own players. Hajduk had a chance from a dead ball themselves in the 42nd minute, winning a free kick some 20 meters from the visitors’ goal — a big opportunity for Šego to add another set-piece goal to his tally.

The first half at Poljud came to a close in the 45+3rd minute. Hajduk have been much the better side on the pitch, going at Raków aggressively from the very first minute and keeping up that intensity right up until the whistle. Still, the biggest chance of the half fell to the visitors, in the closing stages, when Ameyaw’s effort came back off the post.

The second half got underway at Poljud, with the visitors making one change to start the period — Svarnas made way for Debohi.

Hajduk restored their lead in the 47th minute. Šotiček found Dalisson on the edge of the box, and the Spaniard, who had already enjoyed an excellent first half, fired home from 16 meters to send Poljud into another frenzy!

Hajduk went straight on the offensive at the start of the second half. Almost immediately from the restart, in the 48th minute, visiting goalkeeper Trelowski’s pass went straight to Bamba, who fired from around 30 meters, but his effort went wide of the post. Practically from the very next attack, Dalisson was left unmarked on a rebound and blazed his effort over the bar — complete pressure and offensive intent from Hajduk at the start of the half.

Hajduk’s afternoon took a turn for the worse in the 55th minute, however, when Pajaziti committed a heavy foul just around the halfway line. Referee Očenaš didn’t hesitate, showing him a straight red card. Hajduk will have to see out the rest of the match with ten men.

In the 65th minute, the visitors worked an opening for Pienko, but his effort was comfortably dealt with by Silić. Hajduk made a triple change in the 68th minute: Bamba was replaced by Šutalo, while Dalisson, scorer of the second goal, also made way, with Dario Melnjak coming on in his place. Slightly earlier, Gonzalo Garcia had already replaced Šotiček with Del Moral, who took over Pajaziti’s role on the pitch.

In the 72nd minute, Šutalo tried his luck from a half-chance on the counter, but his effort went over the crossbar. During the buildup to that move, the referee had played advantage following a foul on Melnjak, but then failed to book the offending visiting player once the phase of play was over — much to the frustration of the Split supporters.

In the 76th minute, Šego, scorer of the first goal, made way, along with Hrgović, with Marko Livaja and Alec van Hoorenbeeck coming on in their place. Tempers flared on the pitch in the 81st minute after the referee failed to award a foul by Pienko in midfield. Marešić reacted furiously towards Pienko in the aftermath, and it was ultimately the visiting player who ended up picking up a yellow card for the incident.

In the 82nd minute, Livaja let fly from around 20 meters towards the near corner, though Trelowski, not entirely without difficulty, managed to tame the shot. Pienko then tested Silić with an awkward header in the 90th minute, but the Hajduk goalkeeper made a confident save, gathering the ball safely into his grasp. Five minutes of stoppage time were added, and all Hajduk had to do was hold on.

But then the inevitable happened. In the 90+5th minute, Hajduk suffered a last-gasp blow. Once again, the Split side conceded deep into stoppage time to hand Raków a share of the spoils. The game ended 2-2 and the second leg is played in one week.

World.title: Croatia No Longer Near European Bottom in Terms of Annual Leave Affordability
World.content:
August the 20th, 2026 – Croatia is no longer near the European bottom in terms of annual leave affordability, but there are still serious issues with the overall standard of living.

At first glance the figure does not speak in favour of the standard of living in Croatia, however, the picture changes significantly when a longer period is looked at instead of a single year. This was pointed out by economist Ivica Brkljača and reported on by Edita Vlahovic Zuvela.

Almost a third of Croatian citizens over the age of 16 could not afford a week of annual leave outside their place of residence last year. According to the latest Eurostat data, 32.6 percent of the population were in this situation in 2025, placing Croatia seventh among European Union member states with the highest share of citizens for whom such a holiday is not financially accessible.

At first glance, this is a figure that does not speak in favour of the standard of living in Croatia. However, the picture changes significantly when a longer period is considered instead of a single year. Economic analyst Ivica Brkljača draws attention to precisely this, arguing that the 2025 figure should not be viewed in isolation. “The problem arises when this figure is observed in isolation, without the trend that shows how the affordability of annual leave has changed during the period of economic growth,” Brkljača stresses.

recession and recovery

In Croatia, this trend is particularly pronounced. In 2015 as many as 65.8 percent of the population could not afford a week of holiday away from home. Ten years later that share has almost halved, to 32.6 percent. This is an improvement of as much as 33.2 percentage points – the largest among all EU member states. For comparison, Cyprus follows with a drop of 25.9 percentage points, Ireland with 21.6, Bulgaria with 21.3 and Poland with 19.5 percentage points. Croatia’s position relative to the European average has also improved. In 2015 Croatia was the second-worst EU member state, right after Romania. The share of citizens who could not afford annual leave was then a full 30.6 percentage points higher than the EU average, Brkljača recalls. Last year Croatia was the seventh-worst EU member according to this indicator, while the gap to the European average has narrowed to 5.1 percentage points.

a lack of benefit equality

The biggest problem remains among the elderly and single people. Last year as many as 62.6 percent of people over 65 could not afford a week of holiday.

At the level of the entire European Union long-term progress is also visible. In 2015, 35.2 percent of the population could not afford a week of holiday away from home, while last year that share stood at 27.5 percent. Over ten years the share decreased in as many as 23 of the 27 member states, while increases were recorded only by Austria, Germany, Finland and Sweden. The enormous progress that has taken place in Croatia is further illustrated by Brkljača with data available since 2010, the first year for which figures exist for Croatia. The most difficult situation was in 2012, when as many as 71.4 percent of the population could not afford a week of holiday away from home. Very high shares persisted in the following years as well, and then, in parallel with the end of the prolonged recession and the start of economic recovery, almost continuous improvement followed.

Particularly interesting is the movement among households with dependent children. In 2012 as many as 71.3 percent of people from such households could not afford a week of holiday, and in 2015 the figure was 64 percent. Last year their share fell to 24.2 percent. Ten years ago almost two-thirds of such households could not finance a week of holiday, while today the figure is about a quarter.

croatia hasn’t yet reached the sort of living standard it should aspire to

One of the reasons for such pronounced improvement is probably the fact that it mainly concerns the working-age population, which has more directly felt the strong growth in employment and wages. However, economic growth has not affected all groups equally strongly. The biggest problem remains among the elderly and single people. Last year as many as 62.6 percent of people over 65 who live alone could not afford a week of holiday. Among women living alone that share was 57.9 percent, and among men 45 percent.

The number of children in the household is also not unimportant. Around 15 percent of households with one or two children cannot afford a week of holiday, while among those with three or more children the share rises to 33.1 percent. “The growth of GDP, wages and pensions has certainly been felt in the mentioned indicator, as well as in other indicators of the material position of households,” Brkljača concludes. This does not, of course, mean that Croatia has reached the level of living standard it should aspire to. But the trend is hard to ignore: over the past ten years Croatia has achieved the largest reduction in the share of the population that cannot afford a week of holiday among all EU member states.

prices and cost of living are the major determinants

Data from a survey conducted by Alma Career Croatia, the company that runs the MojPosao/MyJob portal, shows a somewhat more cautious picture for this year – more and more employees are planning shorter holidays, and the share of those who will not travel at all this summer is also rising. The share of employees who plan to use a maximum of seven days of annual leave has increased from 15 to 21 percent, while the share of those planning to rest for 21 days or longer has almost halved – from seven to only three percent.

The biggest change concerns those who do not plan to travel at all this summer. Their share has risen from 27 to 32 percent. In other words, almost every third respondent will not go on a summer holiday, primarily because of money. Among those who do not plan to travel, as many as 60 percent cite lack of money as the main reason, compared with 56 percent a year earlier.

Long-term Eurostat data also shows some major progress: the possibility of affording a week of holiday is significantly greater today than ten or fifteen years ago. However, the current survey of employees shows that prices and the cost of living still strongly determine how citizens will spend the summer. Croatia has therefore taken a big step forward, but the benefits of economic growth are not equally distributed. For some pensioners, single people and larger families, a holiday away from home remains a cost that is difficult to fit into the household budget.

World.title: Beijing and Zagreb Connected by a Frequent Airline for the First Time
World.content:
August the 20th, 2026 – Beijing and Zagreb are now connected by a frequent airline for the first time, and tickets are already on sale.

Sinisa Malus writes for Poslovni that China is ready to launch its new route between Beijing and Zagreb via Bucharest on 4 September, which will be the first regular air connection between China and Croatia. Speaking at an event at the Romanian Embassy in Beijing, the president of China National Aviation Holding, Cui Xiaofeng, said that the new route “will further strengthen and enrich Air China’s network in the Central and Eastern European market,” while at the same time establishing a more convenient air bridge for trade, economic cooperation, cultural ties and people-to-people exchanges between China and Croatia.

tickets are already on sale

Air China announced that the route is part of its strategy to deepen its presence in Central and Eastern Europe and further expand its international network, reports Ex-Yu Aviation News. The Chinese carrier also commented on the three-hour stop in Bucharest, noting that the relatively long wait will allow passengers continuing to Zagreb to complete passport control formalities there, meaning they will not have to do so upon arrival in the Croatian capital. Air China plans to operate year-round services between the three cities and has already put tickets on sale for the 2027 summer season.

Dario Mihelin, croatian Ambassador to China

I’m convinced that this flight will make it easier for Chinese tourists to travel to Europe, not only to Croatia but also to neighbouring countries. Passengers can book tickets exclusively between Bucharest and Zagreb, although prices on that sector will vary depending on the number of connecting passengers. Chinese tour operators have already started selling tourist packages for Croatia that include the new flights. During the upcoming winter season, Air China will offer 34,980 seats on its routes to Zagreb. Croatian Ambassador to China Dario Mihelin stressed that this is truly a historic moment for Croatia, as China and Croatia, or rather the capitals Beijing and Zagreb, will for the first time be connected by a regular year-round air route.

an opportunity for not only croatia but the immediate region

“I’m sure that without the coronavirus pandemic, this flight would certainly have been launched much earlier, given that almost half a million Chinese visitors already came to Croatia in 2019. That same year we were already discussing a feasibility study for this flight with representatives of a number of airlines, including Air China,” Mihelin said.

The ambassador added that this route will contribute to better people-to-people connections, strengthening not only tourism cooperation but also economic relations and trade between Croatia and China. “I’m of the belief that this flight will make it easier for Chinese tourists to travel to Europe, not only to Croatia but also to neighbouring countries, such as Slovenia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Montenegro,” Mihelin concluded.

World.title: Zagreb Invests Over 3 Million Euros in Tram Track Renovation
World.content:
August the 20th, 2026 – As Zagreb invests over 3 million euros in tram track renovation, it seems that work to get them completed quickly will see boots on the ground at night, at weekends and even on holidays.

Poslovni reports that the procurement procedure also includes four stationary devices for lubricating tram rails, including their delivery, installation, commissioning and functional testing. For the repair of tram tracks, the City plans to allocate 3.1 million euros. A public procurement is being prepared for works on tram infrastructure, ranging from the replacement of damaged concrete elements and cover plates to the arrangement of tracks and surfaces along the rails. The work would be ordered successively over two years, depending on the condition of the tracks and needs on the ground.

The City of Zagreb plans to conclude a framework agreement with several economic operators, and when the need for a specific intervention is established, the contractor will receive a written request. Work must then begin no later than within 36 hours, and individual contracts may last up to 12 months.

The City is conducting the procedure for ZET, and the documentation provides for the possibility of carrying out works during the day, but also at night, from 22:00-06:00, with slowed or completely suspended tram traffic. Contractors must be prepared to work on weekends and holidays as well, while works may take place simultaneously at a maximum of three locations.

According to the bill of quantities, there will be no shortage of work. Planned, among other things, is the dismantling of around 2,800 reinforced concrete cover plates, while 3,300 are planned to be installed. The removal of 2,500 concrete elements and the installation of 2,000 new ones is also envisaged. The works include the renovation of elements along the rails, their fastening and levelling, after which the track will again be closed with reinforced concrete plates, asphalt concrete or crushed stone, Večernji list reports.

The interventions also cover surfaces between and along the rails. The removal of a total of 2,200 square metres of the existing base layer is planned, as well as the asphalting of 2,000 square metres of roadway surfaces and an additional 100 square metres of pedestrian surfaces. On sections of the tracks where the track is closed with concrete and asphalt, the removal of around 500 cubic metres of existing fill and the construction of a new one is planned. Works will also be carried out on the crushed-stone base and track fill, in a total quantity of 200 cubic metres.

The procurement also includes four stationary devices for lubricating tram rails, including their delivery, installation, commissioning and functional testing. The City notes that the quantities in the bill of quantities are indicative, so the actual quantities executed, as well as the final cost, may be higher or lower than planned.

It should also be recalled that works are currently entering the final phase at the intersection of Savska and Vukovarska streets, one of Zagreb’s busiest junctions. Since the beginning of July, tram switches and crossings have been being replaced there, and according to the City’s latest available data, the asphalt wearing course has been completed on the greater part of the intersection.

At the same time, a major reconstruction of the tram track in Zvonimirova Street is underway. According to the latest status from the construction site, all earthworks have been completed, around 50 percent of the new rails have been laid, and the concreting of the reinforced concrete slab is currently being carried out. This will be followed by backfilling with crushed stone and the continuation of laying the new track. In addition to the main section of Zvonimirova, works are also being carried out at the intersection with Šubićeva Street, where the reconstruction of the worn-out track structure, including the replacement of a tram switch, began in mid-July.

World.title: Madise's supporters to submit her candidacy on Monday
World.content:
On Friday morning, the period during which members of the Riigikogu can submit presidential candidates officially began, but Ülle Madise's supporters plan to deliver her documents to the National Electoral Committee only on Monday.

Reform Party faction chair Õnne Pillak said that the delay has several practical reasons.

On one hand, not all Riigikogu members who have expressed support for Madise have been able to sign her submission yet, Pillak said, noting that Isamaa was the last party to give its approval for Madise's candidacy.

On the other hand, Pillak said a few additional bureaucratic steps still need to be completed to submit the documents correctly.

According to the Election Service, submitting a candidate requires delivering a proposal to the National Electoral Committee that includes the candidate's first and last name, year, month, and day of birth, the names and signatures of those submitting the candidate, and the date the proposal was prepared.

Ülle Madise met with Reform's Riigikogu faction on Tuesday, August 18. Autor/allikas: Siim Lõvi / ERR

The proposal must include the presidential candidate's handwritten consent to run and confirmation that the candidate meets the legal requirements. It must also include documents proving that the candidate is an Estonian citizen by birth.

Representatives from all four factions that have expressed support for Madise — the Reform Party, Estonia 200, the Social Democratic Party, and Isamaa — as well as independent MPs who support her, are expected to take part in submitting her candidacy.

Registration of candidates for the election of the president began Friday at 9 a.m., and candidates can be submitted for the first round of voting until Monday, August 24, at 6 p.m.

The right to nominate a candidate belongs to at least one‑fifth of the Riigikogu, or 21 members. Each member of the Riigikogu may nominate only one candidate.

The National Electoral Committee will meet on Tuesday, August 25, at 3 p.m. to register the candidates.

The Riigikogu's extraordinary session to elect the president will take place on Wednesday, September 2, 2026, beginning at noon.

World.title: Prime minister preferences split evenly in new August poll
World.content:
Practically the same number of voters prefer Isamaa leader Urmas Reinsalu and Estonian Center Party leader Mihhail Kõlvart as a potential prime minister.

Based on the latest results, Reinsalu is preferred by a rounded 25 percent and Kõlvart by 24 percent, with the difference between their support within one percentage point.

Results are from the first half of August in the monthly survey conducted by the NGO Ühiskonnauuringute Instituut and polling firm Norstat Eesti AS.

16 percent would like EKRE leader Martin Helme as prime minister. 12 percent prefer Lavly Perling, leader of Parempoolsed. 10 percent prefer Reform Party leader Kristen Michal, 9 percent Social Democratic Party (SDE) leader Lauri Läänemets, and 6 percent Eesti 200 leader Kristina Kallas.

The share of respondents supporting Helme has declined somewhat (14 percent in July), but no major changes in prime minister preferences have occurred over the past month, Norstat said in a press release.

Among Parempoolsed supporters, Perling is the most popular (80 percent). Among Isamaa supporters, Reinsalu (76 percent). Among Center Party supporters, Kõlvart (75 percent). Among EKRE supporters, Helme (74 percent). Among Reform Party supporters, Michal (60 percent). Among SDE supporters, Läänemets (55 percent).

Respondents were also asked to choose in situations where only two candidates were available. Candidate pairs were formed based on last month's two most popular candidates and the current prime minister. Respondents were asked to choose between the following pairs: Reinsalu vs. Kõlvart, Reinsalu vs. Michal, and Kõlvart vs. Michal. They were asked: "If you could choose only between two candidates, which of them would be a more suitable prime minister for Estonia?"

If choosing between Reinsalu and Michal, 51 percent would prefer Reinsalu and 24 percent Michal. Twenty‑four percent answered "Don't know."

If choosing between Kõlvart and Michal, 45 percent would prefer Kõlvart and 33 percent Michal. Twenty‑two percent answered "Don't know."

If choosing between Reinsalu and Kõlvart, 51 percent would prefer Reinsalu and 32 percent Kõlvart. Seventeen percent answered "Don't know."

Norstat conducted the survey August 10–15, and a total of 1,000 Estonian citizens aged 18 and older responded. To ensure a representative sample, the survey used a combined method — telephone interviews and online surveys, with telephone respondents forming the majority. The sample data were weighted according to the proportional distribution of eligible voters based on key sociodemographic characteristics.
